title: Practice Exam 10
description: An additional full-length 36-question simulated California Class C knowledge exam. Challenging level.

questions.question: You're entering a freeway and the acceleration lane is short. The biggest mistake you can make is to:
choices: Enter the freeway well below traffic speed, forcing others to brake
Match traffic speed before merging
Signal early and check your blind spot
Pick a safe gap to merge into
questions.explanation: Merging far below traffic speed is dangerous—use the ramp to reach traffic speed so you can blend into a gap, even when the ramp is short.

questions.question: You're in the carpool lane and must exit the freeway soon. You should:
choices: Exit the HOV lane where the line is dashed and merge right in stages, early
Wait until your exit, then cut across all lanes
Cross the double lines whenever convenient
Stop and wait for a gap
questions.explanation: Leave the HOV lane only where the line is broken, then change lanes one at a time toward your exit. Plan the moves well ahead.

questions.question: Your tire blows out on the freeway and the car pulls hard to one side. You should:
choices: Hold the wheel firmly, ease off the gas, and steer straight before slowing to the shoulder
Brake hard right away
Let go of the wheel briefly
Accelerate to regain control
questions.explanation: Grip the wheel, take your foot off the gas, and keep the car straight; brake gently only after it slows, then ease onto the shoulder.

questions.question: At a sobriety checkpoint you are lawfully arrested for DUI. The implied consent law means you:
choices: Must submit to a breath or blood test or face automatic license suspension
May refuse all testing with no consequence
Can choose to be tested next week
Are exempt if you were under the limit
questions.explanation: By driving you consented to chemical testing after a lawful DUI arrest. Refusal results in an automatic suspension plus added penalties.

questions.question: How does alcohol most affect your driving even at low levels?
choices: It slows reaction time and impairs judgment, vision, and coordination
It sharpens reflexes
It improves night vision
It has no effect below 0.08%
questions.explanation: Alcohol degrades reaction time, judgment, vision, and coordination starting at low levels—long before the 0.08% legal threshold.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Effects of Alcohol

questions.question: A safe driver treats a hands-free phone conversation as:
choices: Still a distraction—best avoided, with calls saved for when stopped
Completely risk-free
Safer than talking to a passenger
Required to pass the time
questions.explanation: Hands-free is legal for adults but still mentally distracting. When possible, save calls for when you're safely stopped.

questions.question: You're driving and feel the urge to check a notification on your phone. The safest habit is to:
choices: Leave the phone alone until you've parked—silence or 'Do Not Disturb' helps
Glance at it quickly at speed
Check it at the next red light
Hold it low and read while driving
questions.explanation: Use 'Do Not Disturb While Driving' and leave the phone untouched until parked. Even quick glances or red-light checks are risky and largely illegal.

questions.question: A driver under 18 may use a wireless device while driving:
choices: Only to contact emergency services
Hands-free for calls and navigation
For texting at red lights
Any way an adult can
questions.explanation: Provisional (under-18) drivers may not use any wireless device while driving except for a genuine emergency, even hands-free.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Teen Cell Phone Restrictions

questions.question: A steady yellow light means the signal is about to turn red. You should:
choices: Stop if you can do so safely; if you're too close, continue with caution
Always speed up to beat the red
Always slam on the brakes
Treat it like a flashing yellow
questions.explanation: Yellow is a warning to stop if you safely can. Only continue through if stopping would be unsafe (risking a rear-end collision).
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Traffic Signal Lights

questions.question: A red ball with a green left arrow is displayed. Cross traffic and oncoming traffic for the left turn are:
choices: Stopped, giving you a protected left turn
Free to proceed against you
Required to yield to you only if they see you
Unaffected by your signal
questions.explanation: A green left arrow means a protected turn—oncoming traffic faces a red, so you can turn left. Watch for pedestrians and finish before the arrow ends.

questions.question: A signal is completely dark at a busy intersection during a blackout. The safest assumption is:
choices: Treat it as an all-way stop and proceed in turn
The biggest road has the right of way
Drive through without stopping
Wait until power is restored
questions.explanation: A dark signal must be treated as a four-way (all-way) stop. Stop, then take turns proceeding when it's safe.

questions.question: You're in a lane that a sign says will become 'EXIT ONLY' ahead, but you want to stay on the freeway. You should:
choices: Merge left out of that lane before the exit-only section begins
Stay in the lane; you can change your mind at the exit
Stop at the gore and back up
Straddle the lane line
questions.explanation: An exit-only lane leaves the freeway. Merge left early, while you still can, if you intend to continue.

questions.question: Before changing lanes you check your mirror and it looks clear, but you should still:
choices: Turn your head to check the blind spot the mirror can't show
Move over immediately
Rely on the mirror alone
Honk before moving
questions.explanation: Mirrors miss a blind spot big enough to hide a car or motorcycle. A quick head turn confirms the lane is truly clear before you move.

questions.question: A solid yellow line next to a broken yellow line, with the solid line on your side, means:
choices: You may not pass; oncoming traffic on the broken-line side may
You may pass when clear
Both directions may pass
Neither direction may pass
questions.explanation: The line on YOUR side governs you: a solid line means no passing. The opposing side with a broken line may pass.

questions.question: A regulatory white sign reads 'ONE WAY' with an arrow. You must:
choices: Travel only in the direction of the arrow
Yield to oncoming traffic
Treat the street as two-way at night
Stop before entering
questions.explanation: A 'ONE WAY' sign means all traffic moves in the arrow's direction. Never enter or drive against it.

questions.question: A yellow diamond sign shows a red car and a black car with arrows pointing toward each other on a divided line. This warns of:
choices: A two-way traffic section ahead (a divided road becomes two-way)
A passing zone
A merge from the right
A one-way street
questions.explanation: This sign warns that a divided highway is ending and you'll meet two-way traffic. Keep right and don't pass where unsafe.

questions.question: A diamond-shaped yellow sign showing a merging arrow from the right means:
choices: Traffic may enter from the right ahead; adjust speed or position to allow merging
You must exit to the right
The right lane ends and you must merge right
No trucks in the right lane
questions.explanation: A merge warning tells you another road joins ahead. Be ready for entering traffic and cooperate to let it blend in safely.

questions.question: At 65 mph, the 3-second following rule corresponds to roughly:
choices: About 285 feet of space
Two car lengths
About 65 feet
One car length per 5 mph
questions.explanation: At ~65 mph you cover about 95 feet per second, so 3 seconds is roughly 285 feet. The time rule scales with speed; fixed car-lengths don't.

questions.question: When you are being tailgated, increasing your own following distance helps because it:
choices: Lets you brake gradually, giving the tailgater more time to react
Makes the tailgater back off instantly
Allows you to brake harder
Has no real effect
questions.explanation: A bigger gap ahead means any slowdown can be gentle and gradual, reducing the chance the tailgater rear-ends you.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Being Followed Too Closely

questions.question: Your headlights show about 350 feet ahead at night. To avoid 'overdriving' your lights you should keep a speed at which you can stop within:
choices: That lit distance
Twice that distance
Any distance you choose
Half that distance plus reaction time
questions.explanation: Drive slow enough to stop within the distance your headlights reveal. Going faster means you can't stop for something that suddenly appears in range.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Driving at Night

questions.question: On a wet freeway at high speed your steering suddenly feels light and unresponsive. You are likely:
choices: Hydroplaning—ease off the gas and hold the wheel steady
Out of fuel—accelerate
Experiencing brake fade—brake harder
Fine—maintain speed
questions.explanation: Light, vague steering on standing water signals hydroplaning. Lift off the accelerator gently and keep the wheel steady until the tires regrip; prevent it by slowing in the rain.

questions.question: Posted limits assume ideal conditions. On a crowded, rainy night, a safe speed is:
choices: Often below the posted limit, based on traffic and visibility
Exactly the posted limit
Above the limit to keep up with the brave drivers
Whatever the car ahead is doing
questions.explanation: The Basic Speed Law requires adjusting to conditions. Crowding, rain, and darkness usually call for a speed below the posted maximum.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Basic Speed Law

questions.question: The maximum speed when towing a trailer on a California freeway is:
choices: 55 mph
65 mph
70 mph
60 mph
questions.explanation: Vehicles towing trailers are limited to 55 mph statewide, regardless of a higher posted limit for cars.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Speed Limits for Trailers

questions.question: You park parallel on the right side of a two-way street. Your car must face:
choices: The same direction as traffic on your side of the street
Oncoming traffic
Either direction is fine
Toward the curb at an angle
questions.explanation: Park headed in the direction of travel, within 18 inches of the right curb. Parking against traffic (facing oncoming cars) is illegal.

questions.question: It is illegal to park your car:
choices: On a freeway except in a real emergency
In a metered space with time paid
In your own driveway
In a marked, unrestricted space
questions.explanation: Stopping or parking on a freeway is prohibited except for a genuine emergency. Move to the shoulder only if you must, and exit away from traffic.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Where You May Not Park

questions.question: You park downhill with a curb. The correct wheel position is:
choices: Front wheels turned toward the curb
Front wheels turned away from the curb
Front wheels straight
Front wheels toward the road
questions.explanation: Downhill with a curb, turn the wheels toward the curb so a forward roll is stopped by it. Set the parking brake as well.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Parking on Hills

questions.question: An ambulance with siren is stuck behind you in heavy traffic with nowhere for you to go. You should:
choices: Move toward the edge as space allows and stop, making a path when you can
Run the red light ahead to clear out
Stay exactly where you are and do nothing
Speed up through traffic
questions.explanation: Do your best to create a path—edge toward the side as gaps open and stop—without running red lights or making unsafe moves.

questions.question: It is illegal to follow within 300 feet of:
choices: An emergency vehicle running its siren or flashing lights
Any passenger car
A slow-moving truck
A school bus with amber lights
questions.explanation: You must stay more than 300 feet back from a fire engine, ambulance, or police vehicle operating its siren or lights.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Following Emergency Vehicles

questions.question: Two vehicles reach a four-way stop at the same time, directly across from each other. Both go straight. They should:
choices: Both proceed carefully, since their paths don't cross
Wait for each other indefinitely
Yield to the one on the right
Let the larger vehicle go first
questions.explanation: Opposing cars both going straight don't conflict, so both may proceed. Conflicts arise only when one turns across the other's path.

questions.question: You're at a stop sign waiting to turn right; a pedestrian is crossing the street you want to enter. You should:
choices: Wait for the pedestrian to clear your path before turning
Turn behind them quickly
Turn in front of them
Edge forward to make them stop
questions.explanation: Yield to pedestrians crossing the road you're turning into. Wait until they've safely cleared your path before completing the turn.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Turning and Pedestrians

questions.question: A school bus ahead has amber lights flashing, then switches to red with the stop arm out. The amber-to-red change tells you:
choices: The bus has gone from 'about to stop' to 'stopped—you must stop too'
You may now pass quickly
The bus is pulling back into traffic
Only the bus driver needs to act
questions.explanation: Amber means it's preparing to stop; red flashers and the extended stop arm mean stop and stay stopped while children load or cross.

questions.question: A reduced school-zone speed limit is in force when:
choices: Children are present (or as the sign and any flashing beacon indicate)
Only between 8 a.m. and 9 a.m.
At all hours, every day
Only on the first day of school
questions.explanation: School-zone limits apply when children are present, as posted—often reinforced by a flashing beacon during arrival and dismissal times. When in doubt, slow down.

questions.question: Driving near a playground or park, the safest mindset is to:
choices: Expect a child to run out and be ready to stop at any moment
Assume children will stay on the grass
Maintain speed and rely on your horn
Watch only the crosswalks
questions.explanation: Children near parks are unpredictable. Reduce speed, scan widely, and be prepared to stop suddenly.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Watching for Children

questions.question: A bicyclist ahead is riding in the right portion of a wide lane. To pass, you should:
choices: Wait for a clear, safe moment and pass leaving at least 3 feet of space
Pass immediately within the same lane, close to them
Honk and pass at speed
Tailgate until they pull over
questions.explanation: Give at least 3 feet when passing a bicyclist. If the lane is too narrow to do so, wait for a safe opportunity to move over.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Sharing the Road with Bicyclists

questions.question: A pedestrian who is blind steps to the curb and extends a white cane toward the street. You should:
choices: Stop well back and let them cross; they have the right of way
Honk so they know you're there
Drive slowly past in front of them
Proceed because they haven't entered the road yet
questions.explanation: Extending the cane signals intent to cross. Stop well back, stay quiet, and let the pedestrian cross—they always have the right of way.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Pedestrians with Disabilities

questions.question: When a crosswalk is unmarked at an intersection (no painted lines), pedestrians:
choices: Still have the right to cross, and you must yield to them
Have no right to cross there
Must find a marked crosswalk
May cross only with a signal
questions.explanation: A legal crosswalk exists at intersections even without paint. Yield to pedestrians crossing in these unmarked crosswalks just as you would at marked ones.
